extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, district and appellate judges, patent prosecutors, and IP practitioners working on U.S. design patent cases
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and judicial guidance for determining infringement, claim construction, and related inquiries in U.S. design patent litigation—focusing on the ordinary observer test, the role of prior art, and whether the point-of-novelty test should be treated as a separate requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary observer test (Gorham)
rubrics_metrics.description: If, in the eye of an ordinary observer, giving such attention as a purchaser usually gives, two designs are substantially the same such that the resemblance is such as to deceive such an observer (inducing him to purchase one supposing it to be the other), the first one patented is infringed by the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the ordinary observer standard; the observer is not an expert but a purchaser who gives the usual attention. The observer's perspective may and should be informed by the prior art (see below). Identity of appearance or sameness of effect upon the eye is the key inquiry; slight variances in detail do not destroy substantial identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of the point-of-novelty test
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically a separate second test requiring that the accused device appropriate the novelty in the patented device which distinguishes it from the prior art (Litton and progeny).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court disapproves treating the point-of-novelty test as a separate free-standing requirement distinct from the ordinary observer test. Instead, the ordinary observer test should be applied as informed by the prior art so that the factfinder naturally focuses on the aspects that distinguish the patented design from the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of prior art in infringement comparison (three-way comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison should consider the patented design, the accused design, and the closest or relevant prior art designs to determine whether an ordinary observer (familiar with the prior art) would be deceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and factfinders should use the prior art as the frame of reference. Where the prior art is close or the field crowded, small differences between claimed and accused designs may be significant. The accused infringer bears the burden of production to introduce comparison prior art; the patentee retains the ultimate burden to prove infringement by a preponderance of the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-trivial advance test (panel formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A test adopted by a panel (in this case) that a combination of individually known design elements can constitute a point of novelty only if the combination is a non-trivial advance over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court declines to adopt the non-trivial advance test as a requirement for infringement, explaining that it improperly conflates infringement analysis with obviousness and is unnecessary if the ordinary observer test is applied with reference to the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of a crowded art (narrow range of equivalents)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a field is crowded with many references relating to the design of the same type of article, the scope of equivalents afforded a design patent must be construed narrowly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In crowded arts, courts should construe patent scope narrowly and small differences are more likely to prevent a finding of infringement; the composite of differences may present a different overall impression to the ordinary observer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/utilitarian limitation (dictated by utilitarian purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patented design may be invalid if the appearance is dictated solely by utilitarian purpose (design governed by function rather than ornamentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should assess and distinguish between ornamental and purely functional elements (see Oddzon). If a design's appearance is dictated by function (Seiko Epson cited), it may be invalid; functional features do not broaden claim scope for ornamental protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction approach for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents typically are claimed as shown in drawings, and the illustration is often the best description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trial courts are not required to provide a detailed verbal construction of a design patent in the manner used for utility patents; providing drawings as the primary claim medium is generally preferable. Courts have discretion on the level of verbal description—avoid undue verbal elaboration that may over-emphasize particular features and distract the factfinder from the design as a whole. Absent prejudice, issuing a more detailed verbal construction is not reversible error.

rubrics_metrics.name: When verbal description is required for obviousness/invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining obviousness (invalidity), trial courts must attempt to translate visual descriptions into words to communicate the reasoning behind the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translating visual elements into verbal descriptions is required for explaining invalidity analyses (Durling), but that requirement is distinct from and does not mandate detailed verbal claim construction for infringement inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of production and ultimate burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The accused infringer bears the burden of production to introduce prior art for purposes of comparison in the infringement inquiry; the patentee bears the ultimate burden to prove infringement by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accused infringers, having the motivation to point out close prior art, should produce comparison prior art; but introduction of prior art does not shift the patentee's ultimate evidentiary burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court guidance to factfinder without invading factfinding role
rubrics_metrics.description: A trial court may point out features of the claimed design as they relate to the accused design and prior art, and describe conventions or prosecution history, but must avoid unduly invading the jury's fact-finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible guidance includes pointing out that the patented design has pads on three sides while the accused product has pads on four; courts can describe conventions (e.g., broken lines), prosecution history effects, and functionality distinctions. Appellate courts should be cautious about over-prescriptive guidance that interferes with the trial court's discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of drafting conventions and prosecution history
rubrics_metrics.description: Features like broken lines and statements made during prosecution can affect the scope of a design patent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should assess the role of broken lines (37 C.F.R. § 1.152) and any representations in the prosecution history (see Goodyear) when construing the scope of the claimed design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability/inventiveness standard for designs (Whitman Saddle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patentability requires invention or an exercise of the inventive/originative faculty; mere selection/adaptation of existing forms without more is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While this is a patentability standard rather than an infringement test, the analysis of what made a design patentable (the inventive feature) can inform the infringement inquiry when viewed in light of the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating infringement and obviousness inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests or formulations that effectively apply obviousness-type analysis (e.g., non-trivial advance as a separate infringement requirement) conflate infringement and invalidity doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should not use metrics that improperly mix the obviousness inquiry into the infringement analysis; instead use the ordinary observer standard framed by the prior art to capture the concerns non-trivial-advance sought to address without merging doctrinal standards.
